Weighing in at about 350 grams [Wwb = about 350 grams] at birth, the neonate of the Sri Lankan spotted chevrotain enters the world as a highly precocious fawn, capable of standing and following its mother within hours of parturition. This modest initial mass, at the upper end of the reported range of 288 to 382 grams observed in zoological collections, reflects an evolutionary strategy favoring rapid postnatal mobility to evade predators in the dense understory of Sri Lankan forests. The suckling juvenile relies entirely on its mother’s milk during the first weeks, a period of intense somatic growth that sets the stage for the subsequent transition to solid forage.

Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of this tropical species, where an active body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C] is maintained, the duration of gestation in the Sri Lankan spotted chevrotain has been documented at 150 days [tg = 150 days], a figure consistent with the lower bound of the 150- to 160-day range reported in the Animal Diversity Web. This relatively short gestation for a mammal of its size, ending with the delivery of a single, well-developed fawn, likely represents an adaptation that minimizes the metabolic burden on the gravid female while still producing a precocial offspring. The birth event itself is rapid and occurs in a secluded thicket, after which the neonate is quickly licked clean and stimulated to stand.

Weaning, defined as the cessation of suckling and the complete transition to solid food, occurs at 50 days after birth [tx = 50 days after birth] in this species, a milestone that marks the young individual’s nutritional independence from the lactating female at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. At the point of weaning, the juvenile has reached a wet body mass of 1680 grams [Wwx = 1680 grams], a nearly fivefold increase over its neonatal weight that underscores the efficiency of maternal milk provisioning. This dietary transition to browsing on tender leaves, fallen fruits, and herbaceous shoots coincides with a period of increased vulnerability, as the weaned juvenile must now navigate the forest floor without the protection of constant maternal proximity.

Sexual maturation in the Sri Lankan spotted chevrotain proceeds relatively slowly for a small ungulate, with puberty attained at 244 days after birth [tp = 244 days after birth], a value derived from the commonly cited range of 5 to 8 months at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This prolonged pre-reproductive juvenile phase allows for the complete development of the skeletal frame and the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of future gestation and lactation. The sub-adult mammal, now indistinguishable in pelage from adults, begins to establish a solitary home range, often overlapping with the territories of multiple breeding individuals of the opposite sex.

Adult body mass exhibits marked sexual dimorphism, with females ultimately reaching a maximum recorded wet weight of 3800 grams [Wwi = 3800 grams], substantially exceeding the 3100 grams [Wwi = 3100 grams] attained by males. This reversed size dimorphism, unusual among tragulids, may relate to the selective pressures of a polygynous mating system where larger females achieve higher fecundity. The maximum lifespan of the species in the wild is estimated at approximately 14.5 years [am = approximately 14.5 years] under the thermal conditions of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], though captive records suggest occasional individuals may persist beyond this age. Annual reproductive output is modest, with females producing a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter], and approximately 1.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 litters per year], yielding a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 1.5 young per 365 days [Ri = approximately 1.5 young per 365 days] when averaged over the entire reproductive lifespan.
